newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyberspace copyright talks hit fresh snags.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace copyright talks hit fresh snags.

text.p: After nearly three weeks, global talks to rewrite copyright rules for cyberspace were bogged down Thursday, raising doubts that the controversial treaties can be passed by a Friday deadline, negotiators said.

Voting on the treaties was supposed to begin Thursday, but the talks were delayed to allow time to solve disputes between copyright-based industries, such as music, and online companies over exemptions from rules in the digital era.

"It's quite intense. After three weeks of talks, the real meat of the negotiations has really started," said Adrian Strain of the music industry lobbying group, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry.
IFPI's 1,100 members include big record producers BMG Entertainment, EMI Group Plc, Seagram Co. Ltd.'s MCA Music Entertainment Group, Sony Corp.'s Sony Music and PolyGram NV.

Under the auspices of the United Nations' World Intellectual Property Organisation, which coordinates copyrights, the talks cover three treaties -- on literary and artistic works, on rights of performers and producers of music, and on database producers.

They aim to upgrade the century-old Berne convention on copyrights to cover the borderless world of the Internet, which has ripped up the rule books because computer users on the Net can copy and distribute anything from music to software at the click of a mouse.

The music, entertainment and software industries, trying to make sure they profit from works distributed electronically, are enthusiastic supporters of the treaties, which they say provide a legal basis for commercial use of their products on the Internet.
But online and Internet access giants are furious that the treaties make even innocent Web surfing -- which, by definition, requires that a computer make transient copies -- a copyright violation.
Copyright officials say online companies have nothing to fear from the treaties, but the Internet industry wants the treaties to spell out their legal protection.

Internet and online service providers say the pacts expose them to multibillion-dollar liability for copyright violations by millions of service users and give sweeping powers to copyright-based industries like music and entertainment.
They want the most contentious parts deleted altogether.
Telecommunications giants such as Bell Atlantic Corp., America Online Inc. and Nynex Corp. say they cannot police treaties that apply copyright rules to both permanent and temporary reproductions.
The $40-billion-a-year music industry raised the heat in the battle last week, accusing online companies of scaremongering to protect their multibillion-dollar interests.

Online companies for their part allege that music and record companies want to use the Internet as a cash cow, leaving what they say is the impossible task of policing copyright violations under the proposed treaties to the Internet community.
The third treaty on databases is full of confusion and opposed by many sides and is considered dead for the time being, negotiators said.
